entries.da188b662226a3f40201356c843a281f2fedafc2: <div sID="gen17548" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="16" osisID="Jer.16" sID="Jer.16"/> <div eID="gen17548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17549" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17550" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, I. The greatness of the calamity that was coming upon the Jewish nation is illustrated by prohibitions given to the prophet neither to set up a house of his own (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.1-Jer.16.4">ver. 1-4</reference>) nor to go into the house of mourning (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.5-Jer.16.7">ver. 5-7</reference>) nor into the house of feasting, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.8-Jer.16.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>. II. God is justified in these severe proceedings against them by an account of their great wickedness, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.10-Jer.16.13">ver. 10-13</reference>. III. An intimation is given of mercy in reserve, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.14-Jer.16.15">ver. 14, 15</reference>. IV. Some hopes are given that the punishment of the sin should prove the reformation of the sinners, and that they should return to God at length in a way of duty, and so be qualified for his returns to them in a way of favour, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.16-Jer.16.21">ver. 16-21</reference>.
entries.90823fc86ac8d33abf14cbd6414334a3aee8e679: <div eID="gen17550" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17549" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Prohibitions Given to Jeremiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 605.)</title> <div sID="gen17551" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came also unto me, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Thou shalt not take thee a wife, neither shalt thou have sons or daughters in this place. <hi type="super">3</hi> For thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> concerning the sons and concerning the daughters that are born in this place, and concerning their mothers that bare them, and concerning their fathers that begat them in this land; <hi type="super">4</hi> They shall die of grievous deaths; they shall not be lamented; neither shall they be buried; <hi type="italic">but</hi> they shall be as dung upon the face of the earth: and they shall be consumed by the sword, and by famine; and their carcases shall be meat for the fowls of heaven, and for the beasts of the earth. <hi type="super">5</hi> For thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Enter not into the house of mourning, neither go to lament nor bemoan them: for I have taken away my peace from this people, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">even</hi> lovingkindness and mercies. <hi type="super">6</hi> Both the great and the small shall die in this land: they shall not be buried, neither shall <hi type="italic">men</hi> lament for them, nor cut themselves, nor make themselves bald for them: <hi type="super">7</hi> Neither shall <hi type="italic">men</hi> tear <hi type="italic">themselves</hi> for them in mourning, to comfort them for the dead; neither shall <hi type="italic">men</hi> give them the cup of consolation to drink for their father or for their mother. <hi type="super">8</hi> Thou shalt not also go into the house of feasting, to sit with them to eat and to drink. <hi type="super">9</hi> For thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel; Behold, I will cause to cease out of this place in your eyes, and in your days, the voice of mirth, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride. <div eID="gen17551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17552" type="x-p"/> The prophet is here for a sign to the people. They would not regard what he said; let it be tried whether they will regard what he <hi type="italic">does.</hi> In general, he must conduct himself so, in every thing, as became one that expected to see his country in ruins very shortly. This he foretold, but few regarded the prediction; therefore he is to show that he is himself fully satisfied in the truth of it. Others go on in their usual course, but he, in the prospect of these sad times, is forbidden and therefore forbears marriage, mourning for the dead, and mirth. Note, Those that would convince others of and affect them with the word of God must make it appear, even in the most self-denying instances, that they do believe it themselves and are affected with it. If we would rouse others out of their security, and persuade them to sit loose to the world, we must ourselves be mortified to present things and show that we expect the dissolution of them. <div eID="gen17552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17553" type="x-p"/> I. Jeremiah must not marry, nor think of having a family and being a housekeeper (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not take thee a wife,</hi> nor think of <hi type="italic">having sons and daughters in this place,</hi> not in the land of Judah, not in Jerusalem, not in Anathoth. The Jews, more than any people, valued themselves on their early marriages and their numerous offspring. But Jeremiah must live a bachelor, not so much in honour of virginity as in diminution of it. By this it appears that it was advisable and seasonable only in calamitous times, and times of <hi type="italic">present distress,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.26">1 Cor. vii. 26</reference>. That it is so is a part of the calamity. There may be a time when it will be said, <hi type="italic">Blessed is the womb that bears not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.23.29">Luke xxiii. 29</reference>. When we see such times at hand it is wisdom for all, especially for prophets, to keep themselves as much as may be from being <hi type="italic">entangled with the affairs of this life</hi> and encumbered with that which, the dearer it is to them, the more it will be the matter of their care, and fear, and grief, at such a time. The reason here given is because the <hi type="italic">fathers</hi> and <hi type="italic">mothers, the sons and the daughters, shall die of grievous deaths,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.16.3-Jer.16.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. As for those that have wives and children, 1. They will have such a clog upon them that they cannot flee from those deaths. A single man may make his escape and shift for his own safety, when he that has a wife and children can neither find means to convey with them nor find in his heart to go and leave them behind him. 2. They will be in continual terror for fear of those deaths; and the more they have to lose by them the greater will the terror and consternation be when death appears every where in its triumphant pomp and power. 3. The death of every child, and the aggravating circumstances of it, will be a new death to the parent. Better have no children than have them brought forth and bred up <hi type="italic">for the murderer</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.9.13-Hos.9.14">Hos. ix. 13, 14</reference>), than see them live and die in misery. Death is grievous, but some deaths are more grievous than others, both to those that die and to their relations that survive them; hence we read of <hi type="italic">so great a death,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.10">2 Cor. i. 10</reference>. Two things are used a little to palliate and alleviate the terror of death as to this world, and to sugar the bitter pill—bewailing the dead and burying them; but, to make those deaths grievous indeed, these are denied: <hi type="italic">They shall not be lamented,</hi> but shall be carried off, as if all the world were weary of them; nay, they <hi type="italic">shall not be buried,</hi> but left exposed, as if they were designed to be monuments of justice. <hi type="italic">They shall be a dung upon the face of the earth,</hi> not only despicable, but detestable, as if they were good for nothing but to manure the ground; being <hi type="italic">consumed,</hi> some <hi type="italic">by the sword</hi> and some <hi type="italic">by famine, their carcases shall be meat for the fowls of heaven and the beasts of the earth.</hi> Will not any one say, "Better be without children than live to see them come to this?" What reason have we to say,<hi type="italic">All is vanity and vexation of spirit,</hi> when those creatures that we expect to be our greatest comforts may prove not only our heaviest cares, but our sorest crosses! <div eID="gen17553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17554" type="x-p"/> II. Jeremiah must not go to the house of mourning upon occasion of the death of any of his neighbours or relations (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Enter thou not into the house of mourning.</hi> It was usual to condole with those whose relations were dead, to <hi type="italic">bemoan them,</hi> to <hi type="italic">cut themselves,</hi> and <hi type="italic">make themselves bald,</hi> which, it seems, was commonly practised as an expression of mourning, though forbidden by the law, <reference osisRef="Deut.14.1">Deut. xiv. 1</reference>. Nay, sometimes, in a passion of grief, they did <hi type="italic">tear themselves for them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.6-Jer.16.7">v. 6, 7</reference>), partly in honour of the deceased, thus signifying that they thought there was a great loss of them, and partly in compassion to the surviving relations, to whom the burden will be made the lighter by their having sharers with them in their grief. They used to mourn with them, and so <hi type="italic">to comfort them for the dead,</hi> as Job's friends with him and the Jews with Martha and Mary; and it was a friendly office to <hi type="italic">give them a cup of consolation to drink,</hi> to provide cordials for them and press them earnestly to drink of them for the support of their spirits, give wine to those that are of heavy heart <hi type="italic">for their father or mother,</hi> that it may be some comfort to them to find that, though they have lost their parents, yet they have some friends left that have a concern for them. Thus the usage stood, and it was a laudable usage. It is a good work to others, as well as of good use to ourselves, to <hi type="italic">go to the house of mourning.</hi> It seems, the prophet Jeremiah had been wont to abound in good offices of this kind, and it well became his character both as a pious man and as a prophet; and one would think it should have made him better beloved among his people than it should seem he was. But now God bids him not lament the death of his friends as usual, for 1. His sorrow for the destruction of his country in general must swallow up his sorrow for particular deaths. His tears must now be turned into another channel; and there is occasion enough for them all. 2. He had little reason to lament those who died now just before the judgments entered which he saw at the door, but rather to think those happy who were seasonable <hi type="italic">taken away from the evil to come.</hi> 3. This was to be a type of what was coming, when there should be such universal confusion that all neighbourly friendly offices should be neglected. Men shall be in deaths so often, and even dying daily, that they shall have no time, no room, no heart, for the ceremonies that used to attend death. The sorrows shall be so ponderous as not to admit relief, and every one so full of grief for his own troubles that he shall have no thought of his neighbours. All shall be mourners then, and no comforters; every one will find it enough to bear his own burden; for (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.5">v. 5</reference>), "<hi type="italic">I have taken away my peace from this people,</hi> put a full period to their prosperity, deprived them of health, wealth, and quiet, and friends, and every thing wherewith they might comfort themselves and one another." Whatever peace we enjoy, it is God's peace; it is his gift, and, <hi type="italic">if he give quietness, who then can make trouble?</hi> But, if we make not a good use of his peace, he can and will take it away; and where are we then? <reference osisRef="Job.34.29">Job xxxiv. 29</reference>. "I will take away my peace, <hi type="italic">even my loving-kindness and mercies;</hi>" these shall be shut up and restrained, which are the fresh springs from which all their fresh streams flow, and then farewell all good. Note, Those have cut themselves off from all true peace that have thrown themselves out of the favour of God. All is gone when God takes away from us his lovingkindness and his mercies. Then it follows (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.6">v. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">Both the great and the small shall die,</hi> even <hi type="italic">in this land,</hi> the land of Canaan, that used to be called the <hi type="italic">land of the living.</hi> God's favour is our life; take away that, and <hi type="italic">we die, we perish, we all perish.</hi> <div eID="gen17554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17555" type="x-p"/> III. Jeremiah must not go to the house of mirth, any more than to the house of mourning, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.8">v. 8</reference>. It had been his custom, and it was innocent enough, when any of his friends made entertainments at their houses and invited him to them, to <hi type="italic">go and sit with them,</hi> not merely to drink, but <hi type="italic">to eat and to drink,</hi> soberly and cheerfully. But now he must not take that liberty, 1. Because it was unseasonable, and inconsistent with the providences of God in reference to that land and nation. God called aloud to <hi type="italic">weeping, and mourning, and fasting;</hi> he was coming forth against them in his judgments; and it was time for them to <hi type="italic">humble themselves;</hi> and it well became the prophet who gave them the warning to give them an example of taking the warning, and complying with it, and so to make it appear that he did himself believe it. Ministers ought to be examples of self-denial and mortification, and to show themselves affected with those terrors of the Lord with which they desire to affect others. And it becomes all the sons of Zion to sympathize with her in her afflictions, and not to be merry when she is perplexed, <reference osisRef="Amos.6.6">Amos vi. 6</reference>. 2. Because he must thus show the people what sad times were coming upon them. His friends wondered that he would not meet them, as he used to do, in the house of feasting. But he lets them know it was to intimate to them that all their feasting would be at an end shortly (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will cause to cease the voice of mirth.</hi> You shall have nothing to feast on, nothing to rejoice in, but be surrounded with calamities that shall mar your mirth and cast a damp upon it." God can find ways to tame the most jovial. "This shall be done <hi type="italic">in this place,</hi> in Jerusalem, that used to be the <hi type="italic">joyous city</hi> and thought her joys were all secure to her. It shall be done <hi type="italic">in your eyes,</hi> in your sight, to be a vexation to you, who now look so haughty and so merry. It shall be done <hi type="italic">in your days;</hi> you yourselves shall live to see it." The voice of praise they had made to cease by their iniquities and idolatries, and therefore justly God made to cease among them <hi type="italic">the voice of mirth and gladness.</hi> The voice of God's prophets was not heard, was not heeded, among them, and therefore no longer shall <hi type="italic">the voice of the bridegroom and of the bride,</hi> of the songs that used to grace the nuptials, be heard among them. See <reference osisRef="Jer.7.34">ch. vii. 34</reference>.
entries.89c0eb5e199ec069d2b4a2c4898b7ba9f2a300e1: <div eID="gen17555" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Causes of Divine Judgments. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 605.)</title> <div sID="gen17556" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> And it shall come to pass, when thou shalt shew this people all these words, and they shall say unto thee, Wherefore hath the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> pronounced all this great evil against us? or what <hi type="italic">is</hi> our iniquity? or what <hi type="italic">is</hi> our sin that we have committed against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God? <hi type="super">11</hi> Then shalt thou say unto them, Because your fathers have forsaken me, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and have walked after other gods, and have served them, and have worshipped them, and have forsaken me, and have not kept my law; <hi type="super">12</hi> And ye have done worse than your fathers; for, behold, ye walk every one after the imagination of his evil heart, that they may not hearken unto me: <hi type="super">13</hi> Therefore will I cast you out of this land into a land that ye know not, <hi type="italic">neither</hi> ye nor your fathers; and there shall ye serve other gods day and night; where I will not shew you favour. <div eID="gen17556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17557" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. An enquiry made into the reasons why God would bring those judgments upon them (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">When thou shalt show this people all these words,</hi> the words of this curse, they will say unto thee, <hi type="italic">Wherefore has the Lord pronounced all this great evil against us?</hi> One would hope that there were some among them that asked this question with a humble penitent heart, desiring to know what was the sin for which God contended with them, that they might cast it away and prevent the judgment: "Show us the Jonah that raises the storm and we will throw it overboard." But it seems here to be the language of those who quarrelled at the word of God, and challenged him to show what they had done which might deserve so severe a punishment: "<hi type="italic">What is our iniquity? Or what is our sin?</hi> What crime have we even been guilty of, proportionable to such a sentence?" Instead of humbling and condemning themselves, they stand upon their own justification and insinuate that God did them wrong in pronouncing this evil against them, that he <hi type="italic">laid upon them more than was right,</hi> and that they had reason to <hi type="italic">enter into judgment with God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.34.23">Job xxxiv. 23</reference>. Note, It is amazing to see how hardly sinners are brought to justify God and judge themselves when they are in trouble, and to own the iniquity and the sin that have procured them the trouble. 2. A plain and full answer given to this enquiry. Do they ask the prophet why, and for what reason, God is thus angry with them? He shall not stop their mouths by telling them that they may be sure there is a sufficient reason, the righteous God is never <hi type="italic">angry without cause,</hi> without good cause; but he must tell them particularly what is the cause, that they may be convinced and humbled, or at least that God may be justified. Let them know then, (1.) That God visited upon them the iniquities of their fathers (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Your fathers have forsaken me, and have not kept my law.</hi> They shook off divine institutions and grew weary of them (they thought them too plain, too mean), and then they <hi type="italic">walked after other gods,</hi> whose worship was more gay and pompous; and, being fond of variety and novelty, they <hi type="italic">served them and worshipped them;</hi> and this was the sin which God had said, in the second commandment, he would <hi type="italic">visit upon their children,</hi> who kept up these idolatrous usages, because they received them <hi type="italic">by tradition from their fathers,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.18">1 Pet. i. 18</reference>. (2.) That God reckoned with them for their own iniquities (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.12">v. 12</reference>): "You have made your fathers' sin your own, and have become obnoxious to the punishment which in their days was deferred, for <hi type="italic">you have done worse than your fathers.</hi>" If they had made a good use of their fathers' reprieve, and had been led by the patience of God to repentance, they would have fared the better for it and the judgment would have been prevented, the reprieve turned into a national pardon; but, making an ill use of it, and being hardened by it in their sins, they fared the worse for it, and, the reprieve having expired, an addition was made to the sentence and it was executed with the more severity. They were more impudent and obstinate in sin than their fathers, <hi type="italic">walked every one after the imagination of his own heart,</hi> made that their guide and rule and were resolved to follow that, on purpose <hi type="italic">that they might not hearken to God</hi> and his prophets. They designedly suffered their own lusts and passions to be noisy, that they might drown the voice of their consciences. No wonder then that God has taken up this resolution concerning them (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.13">v. 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will cast you out of this land,</hi> this land of light, this valley of vision. Since you will not hearken to me, you shall not hear me; you shall be hurried away, not into a neighbouring country which you have formerly had some acquaintance and correspondence with, but into a far country, <hi type="italic">a land that you know not, neither you nor your fathers,</hi> in which you have no interest, nor can expect to meet with any comfortable society, to be an allay to your misery." Justly were those banished into a strange land who doted upon strange gods, which neither they nor their fathers knew, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.17">Deut. xxxii. 17</reference>. Two things would make their case there very miserable, and both of them relate to the soul, the better part; the greatest calamities of their captivity were those which affected that and debarred that from its bliss. [1.] "It is the happiness of the soul to be employed in the service of God; but <hi type="italic">there shall you serve other gods day and night;</hi> that is, you shall be in continual temptation to serve them and perhaps compelled to do it by your cruel task-masters; and, when you are forced to worship idols, you will be as sick of such worship as ever you were fond of it when it was forbidden you by your godly kings." See how God often makes men's sin their punishment, and <hi type="italic">fills the backslider in heart with his own ways.</hi> "You shall have no public worship at all but the worship of idols, and then you will think with regret how you slighted the worship of the true God." [2.] "It is the happiness of the soul to have some tokens of the lovingkindness of God, but you shall go to a strange land, <hi type="italic">where I will not show you favour.</hi>" If they had had God's favour, that would have made even the land of their captivity a pleasant land; but, if they lie under his wrath, the yoke of their oppression will be intolerable to them.
entries.be04bbc81405820a62644c7eac18e4831adcd2c2: <div eID="gen17557" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Judgment and Mercy; Restoration of the Jews; Deliverance from Babylon. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  605.)</title> <div sID="gen17558" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that it shall no more be said, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> liveth, that brought up the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt; <hi type="super">15</hi> But, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> liveth, that brought up the children of Israel from the land of the north, and from all the lands whither he had driven them: and I will bring them again into their land that I gave unto their fathers. <hi type="super">16</hi> Behold, I will send for many fishers, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and they shall fish them; and after will I send for many hunters, and they shall hunt them from every mountain, and from every hill, and out of the holes of the rocks. <hi type="super">17</hi> For mine eyes <hi type="italic">are</hi> upon all their ways: they are not hid from my face, neither is their iniquity hid from mine eyes. <hi type="super">18</hi> And first I will recompense their iniquity and their sin double; because they have defiled my land, they have filled mine inheritance with the carcases of their detestable and abominable things. <hi type="super">19</hi> <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , my strength, and my fortress, and my refuge in the day of affliction, the Gentiles shall come unto thee from the ends of the earth, and shall say, Surely our fathers have inherited lies, vanity, and <hi type="italic">things</hi> wherein <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no profit. <hi type="super">20</hi> Shall a man make gods unto himself, and they <hi type="italic">are</hi> no gods? <hi type="super">21</hi> Therefore, behold, I will this once cause them to know, I will cause them to know mine hand and my might; and they shall know that my name <hi type="italic">is</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen17558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17559" type="x-p"/> There is a mixture of mercy and judgment in these verses, and it is hard to know to which to apply some of the passages here—they are so interwoven, and some seem to look as far forward as the times of the gospel. <div eID="gen17559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17560" type="x-p"/> I. God will certainly execute judgment upon them for their idolatries. Let them expect it, for the decree has gone forth. 1. God sees all their sins, though they commit them ever so secretly and palliate them ever so artfully (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">My eyes are upon all their ways.</hi> They have not their eye upon God, have no regard to him, stand in no awe of him; but he has his eye upon them; neither they nor their sins are <hi type="italic">hidden from his face, from his eyes.</hi> Note, None of the sins of sinners either can be concealed from God or shall be overlooked by him, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.21">Prov. v. 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.34.21">Job xxxiv. 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.90.8">Ps. xc. 8</reference>. 2. God is highly displeased, particularly at their idolatries, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.18">v. 18</reference>. As his omniscience convicts them, so his justice condemns them: <hi type="italic">I will recompense their iniquity and their sin double,</hi> not double to what it deserves, but double to what they expect and to what I have done formerly. Or I will recompense it <hi type="italic">abundantly;</hi> they shall now pay for their long reprieve and the divine patience they have abused. The sin for which God has a controversy with them is their having <hi type="italic">defiled God's land</hi> with their idolatries, and not only alienated that which he was entitled to as his inheritance, but polluted that which he dwelt in with delight as his inheritance, and made it offensive to him <hi type="italic">with the carcases of their detestable things,</hi> the gods themselves which they worshipped, the images of which, though they were of gold and silver, were as loathsome to God as the putrid carcases of men or beasts are to us. Idols are <hi type="italic">carcases of detestable things.</hi> God hates them, and so should we. Or he might refer to the sacrifices which they offered to these idols, with which <hi type="italic">the land was filled;</hi> for they had high places in all the coasts and corners of it. This was the sin which, above any other, incensed God against them. 3. He will find out and raise up instruments of his wrath, that shall <hi type="italic">cast them out of their land,</hi> according to the sentence passed upon them (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will send for many fishers and many hunters</hi>—the Chaldean army, that shall have many ways of ensnaring and destroying them, by fraud as fishers, by force as hunters. They shall find them out wherever they are, and shall chase and closely pursue them, to their ruin. They shall discover them wherever they are hid, in <hi type="italic">hills</hi> or <hi type="italic">mountains,</hi> or <hi type="italic">holes of the rocks,</hi> and shall drive them out. God has various ways of prosecuting a people with his judgments that avoid the convictions of his word. He has men at command fit for his purpose; he has them within call, and can send for them when he pleases. 4. Their bondage in Babylon shall be sorer and much more grievous than that in Egypt, their task-masters more cruel, and their lives made more bitter. This is implied in the promise (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.14-Jer.16.15">v. 14, 15</reference>), that their deliverance out of Babylon shall be more illustrious in itself, and more welcome to them, than that out of Egypt. Their slavery in Egypt came upon them gradually and almost insensibly; that in Babylon came upon them at once and with all the aggravating circumstances of terror. In Egypt they had a Goshen of their own, but none such in Babylon. In Egypt they were used as servants that were useful, in Babylon as captives that had been hateful. 5. They shall be warned, and God shall be glorified, by these judgments brought upon them. These judgments have a voice, and speak aloud, (1.) Instruction to them. When God chastens them he teaches them. By this rod God expostulates with them (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.20">v. 20</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Shall a man make gods to himself?</hi> Will any man be so perfectly void of all reason and consideration as to think that a god of his own making can stand him in any stead? Will you ever again be such fools as you have been, to make to yourselves gods which are no gods, when you have a God whom you may call your own, who made you, and is himself the true and living God?" (2.) Honour to God; for he will be known by the judgments which he executes. He will first recompense their iniquity (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.18">v. 18</reference>), and then he will <hi type="italic">this once</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.21">v. 21</reference>)—this once for all, not by many interruptions of their peace, but this one desolation and destruction of it. "For <hi type="italic">this once,</hi> and no more, <hi type="italic">I will cause them to know my hand,</hi> the length and weight of my punishing hand, how far it can reach and how deeply it can wound. <hi type="italic">And they shall know that my name is Jehovah,</hi> a God with whom there is no contending, who gives being to threatenings and puts life into them as well as promises." <div eID="gen17560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17561" type="x-p"/> II. Yet he has mercy in store for them, intimations of which come in here for the encouragement of the prophet himself and of those few among them that tremble at God's word. It was said, with an air of severity (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.13">v. 13</reference>), that God would banish them into a strange land; but, that thereby they might not be driven to despair, there follow immediately words of comfort. <div eID="gen17561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17562" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">The days will come,</hi> the joyful days, when the same hand that dispersed them shall gather them again, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.14-Jer.16.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. They are cast out, but they are not cast off, they are not cast away. They shall be <hi type="italic">brought up from the land of the north,</hi> the land of their captivity, where they are held with a strong hand, <hi type="italic">and from all the lands whither they are driven,</hi> and where they seemed to be lost and buried in the crowd; nay, <hi type="italic">I will bring them again into their own land,</hi> and settle them there. As he foregoing threatenings agreed with what was written in this law, so does this promise. <hi type="italic">Yet will I not cast them away,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.44">Lev. xxvi. 44</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thence will the Lord thy God gather thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.30.4">Deut. xxx. 4</reference>. And the following words (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.16">v. 16</reference>) may be understood as a promise; God will send for fishers and hunters, the Medes and Persians, that shall find them out in the countries where they are scattered, and send them back to their own land; or Zerubbabel, and others of their own nation, who should fish them out and hunt after them, to persuade them to return; or whatever instruments the Spirit of God made use of to <hi type="italic">stir up their spirits to go up,</hi> which at first they were backward to do. They began to nestle in Babylon; but, <hi type="italic">as an eagle stirs up her nest and flutters over her young,</hi> so God did by them, <reference osisRef="Zech.2.7">Zech. ii. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen17562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17563" type="x-p"/> 2. Their deliverance out of Babylon should, upon some accounts, be more illustrious and memorable than their deliverance out of Egypt was. Both were the Lord's doing and marvellous in their eyes; both were proofs that the Lord liveth and were to be kept in everlasting remembrance, to his honour, as the living God; but the fresh mercy shall be so surprising, so welcome, that it shall even abolish the memory of the former. Not but that new mercies should put us in mind of old ones, and give us occasion to renew our thanksgivings for them; yet because we are tempted to think that the former days were better than these, and to ask, <hi type="italic">Where are all the wonders that our fathers told us of?</hi> as if God's <hi type="italic">arm</hi> had <hi type="italic">waxed short,</hi> and to cry up the age of miracles above the later ages, when mercies are wrought in a way of common providence, therefore we are allowed here comparatively to forget the bringing of Israel out of Egypt as a deliverance outdone by that out of Babylon. That was done <hi type="italic">by might and power,</hi> this <hi type="italic">by the Spirit of the Lord of hosts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.4.6">Zech. iv. 6</reference>. In this there was more of pardoning mercy (the most glorious branch of divine mercy) than in that; for their captivity in Babylon had more in it of the punishment of sin than their bondage in Egypt; and therefore that which comforts Zion in her deliverance out of Babylon is this, that <hi type="italic">her iniquity is pardoned,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.40.2">Isa. xl. 2</reference>. Note, God glorifies himself, and we must glorify him, in those mercies that have no miracles in them, as well as in those that have. And, though the favours of God to our fathers must not be forgotten, yet those to ourselves in our own day we must especially give thanks for. <div eID="gen17563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17564" type="x-p"/> 3. Their deliverance out of captivity shall be accompanied with a blessed reformation, and they shall return effectually cured of their inclination to idolatry, which will complete their deliverance and make it a mercy indeed. They had defiled their own land with their <hi type="italic">detestable things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.16.18">v. 18</reference>. But, when they have smarted for so doing, they shall come and humble themselves before God, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.19-Jer.16.21">v. 19-21</reference>. (1.) They shall be brought to acknowledge that their God only is God indeed, for he is a God in need—<hi type="italic">"My strength</hi> to support and comfort me, <hi type="italic">my fortress</hi> to protect and shelter me, <hi type="italic">and my refuge</hi> to whom I may flee <hi type="italic">in the day of affliction.</hi>" Note, Need drives many to God who had set themselves at a distance from him. Those that slighted him in the day of their prosperity will be glad to flee to him in the day of their affliction. (2.) They shall be quickened to return to him by the conversion of the Gentiles: <hi type="italic">The Gentiles shall come to thee from the ends of the earth;</hi> and therefore shall not we come? Or, "The Jews, who had by their idolatries made themselves as Gentiles (so I rather understand it), <hi type="italic">shall come to thee</hi> by repentance and reformation, shall return to their duty and allegiance, even <hi type="italic">from the ends of the earth,</hi> from all the countries whither they were driven." The prophet comforts himself with the hope of this, and in a transport of joy returns to God the notice he had given him of it: "<hi type="italic">O Lord! my strength and my fortress,</hi> I am now easy, since thou hast given me a prospect of multitudes that shall <hi type="italic">come to thee from the ends of the earth,</hi> both of Jewish converts and of Gentile proselytes." Note, Those that are brought to God themselves cannot but rejoice greatly to see others coming to him, coming back to him. (3.) They shall acknowledge the folly of their ancestors, which it becomes them to do, when they were smarting for the sins of their ancestors: "<hi type="italic">Surely our fathers have inherited,</hi> not the satisfaction they promised themselves and their children, but <hi type="italic">lies, vanity, and things wherein there is no profit.</hi> We are now sensible that our fathers were cheated in their idolatrous worship; it did not prove what it promised, and therefore what have we to do any more with it?" Note, It were well if the disappointment which some have met with in the service of sin, and the pernicious consequences of it to them, might prevail to deter others from treading in their steps. (4.) They shall reason themselves out of their idolatry; and that reformation is likely to be sincere and durable which results from a rational conviction of the gross absurdity there is in sin. They shall argue thus with themselves (and it is well argued), <hi type="italic">Should a man</hi> be such a fool, so perfectly void of the reason of a man, as to <hi type="italic">make gods to himself,</hi> the creatures of his own fancy, the work of his own hands, when they are really <hi type="italic">no gods?</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.16.20">v. 20</reference>. Can a man be so besotted, so perfectly lost to human understanding, as to expect any divine blessing or favour from that which pretends to no divinity but what it first received from him? (5.) They shall herein give honour to God, and make it to appear that they know both his hand in his providence and his name in his word, and that they are brought to know his name by what they are made to know of his hand, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.21">v. 21</reference>. <hi type="italic">This once,</hi> now at length, they shall be made to know that which they would not be brought to know by all the pains the prophets took with them. Note, So stupid are we that nothing less than the mighty hand of divine grace, known experimentally, can make us know rightly the name of God as it is revealed to us. <div eID="gen17564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17565" type="x-p"/> 4. Their deliverance out of captivity shall be a type and figure of this great salvation to be wrought out by the Messiah, who shall <hi type="italic">gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad.</hi> And this is that which so far outshines the deliverance out of Egypt as even to eclipse the lustre of it, and make it even to be forgotten. To this some apply that of the <hi type="italic">many fishers</hi> and <hi type="italic">hunters,</hi> the preachers of the gospel, who were <hi type="italic">fishers of men,</hi> to enclose souls with the gospel net, to find them out <hi type="italic">in every mountain</hi> and <hi type="italic">hill,</hi> and secure them for Christ. Then the Gentiles came to God, some <hi type="italic">from the ends of the earth,</hi> and turned to the worship of him from the service of dumb idols.  <chapter eID="Jer.16"/> <div eID="gen17565" type="x-p"/>

entries.c7dcb02233e54bf794b9af8b1568660d0a5d48a4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9945"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 16</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.16.1-Jer.16.21">Jr 16:1-21</reference>. Continuation of the Previous Prophecy.</title> <div sID="gen17687" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9945"/><hi type="bold">2. in this place--</hi>in Judea. The direction to remain single was (whether literally obeyed, or only in prophetic vision) to symbolize the coming calamities of the Jews (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.15-Ezek.24.27">Eze 24:15-27</reference>) as so severe that the single state would be then (contrary to the ordinary course of things) preferable to the married (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.8">1Co 7:8</reference>, 26, 29; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.19">Mt 24:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.23.29">Lu 23:29</reference>). <div eID="gen17687" type="x-p"/>
entries.d2e2c9f3aaf41c1d1811ec5f5f34def1e53e4965: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9946"/><div sID="gen17688" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9946"/><hi type="bold">4. grievous deaths--</hi>rather, "deadly diseases" (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.2">Jr 15:2</reference>).<div eID="gen17688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17689" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not ... lamented--</hi>so many shall be the slain (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.18">Jr 22:18</reference>).<div eID="gen17689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17690" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dung--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.83.10">Psa 83:10</reference>). <div eID="gen17690" type="x-p"/>
entries.a03c12d99f1b6541df54c31f2b39372e91e6b42f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9947"/><div sID="gen17691" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9947"/>5. (<reference osisRef="Ezek.24.17">Eze 24:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.23">22, 23</reference>).<div eID="gen17691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17692" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">house of mourning--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Mark.5.38">Mr 5:38</reference>). Margin, "mourning-feast"; such feasts were usual at funerals. The Hebrew means, in <reference osisRef="Amos.6.7">Am 6:7</reference>, the cry of joy at a banquet; here, and <reference osisRef="Lam.2.19">La 2:19</reference>, the cry of sorrow. <div eID="gen17692" type="x-p"/>
entries.1ad9c8dde4f00fd147f97522b412ad51411ca5a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9948"/><div sID="gen17693" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9948"/><hi type="bold">6. cut themselves--</hi>indicating extravagant grief (<reference osisRef="Jer.41.5">Jr 41:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.47.5">47:5</reference>), prohibited by the law (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.28">Le 19:28</reference>).<div eID="gen17693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17694" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bald--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.7.29">Jr 7:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.12">Is 22:12</reference>). <div eID="gen17694" type="x-p"/>
entries.a3411309f7656c6ca9aae0def93187fc20106e40: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9949"/><div sID="gen17695" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9949"/><hi type="bold">7. tear themselves--</hi>rather, "break bread," namely, that eaten at the funeral-feast (<reference osisRef="Deut.26.14">De 26:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.42.11">Job 42:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.17">Eze 24:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.9.4">Ho 9:4</reference>). "Bread" is to be supplied, as in <reference osisRef="Lam.4.4">La 4:4</reference>; compare "take" (food) (<reference osisRef="Gen.42.33">Ge 42:33</reference>).<div eID="gen17695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17696" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">give ... cup of consolation ... for ... father--</hi>It was the Oriental custom for friends to send viands and wine (the "cup of consolation") to console relatives in mourning-feasts, for example, to children upon the death of a "father" or "mother." <div eID="gen17696" type="x-p"/>

entries.6965071422a7cdc2694f58694d2dbb84ae57ed96: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9954"/><div sID="gen17701" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9954"/><hi type="bold">12. ye--</hi>emphatic: so far from avoiding your fathers' bad example, ye have done worse (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.26">Jr 7:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.9">1Ki 14:9</reference>).<div eID="gen17701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17702" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">imagination--</hi>rather, "stubborn perversity."<div eID="gen17702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17703" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that they may not hearken--</hi>rather, connected with "ye"; "ye have walked ... so as not to hearken to Me." <div eID="gen17703" type="x-p"/>
entries.e67c1d43221483ef2993a1b81596fe92de68416d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9955"/><div sID="gen17704" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9955"/><hi type="bold">13. serve other gods--</hi>That which was their sin in their own land was their punishment in exile. Retribution in kind. They voluntarily forsook God for idols at home; they were not allowed to serve God, if they wished it, in captivity (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.12">Da 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.6.7">6:7</reference>).<div eID="gen17704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17705" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">day and night--</hi>irony. You may there serve idols, which ye are so mad after, even to satiety, and without intermission. <div eID="gen17705" type="x-p"/>
entries.5e8c1e0de6b7ac4065730e953ec95f3cc6a18eb7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9956"/><div sID="gen17706" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9956"/><hi type="bold">14. Therefore--</hi>So severe shall be the Jews' bondage that their deliverance from it shall be a greater benefit than that out of Egypt. The consolation is incidental here; the prominent thought is the severity of their punishment, so great that their rescue from it will be greater than that from Egypt [Calvin]; so the context, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.13">Jr 16:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.18">17, 18</reference>, proves (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.7">Jr 23:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.18">Is 43:18</reference>). <div eID="gen17706" type="x-p"/>
entries.e0192634ee0097ca8f92ca14a8fd53dc8c3f494c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9957"/><div sID="gen17707" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9957"/><hi type="bold">15. the north--</hi>Chaldea. But while the return from Babylon is primarily meant, the return hereafter is the full and final accomplishment contemplated, as "from all the lands" proves. "Israel" was not, save in a very limited sense, "gathered from all the lands" at the return from Babylon (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.24.6">Jr 24:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.3">Jr 30:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.15">Jr 32:15</reference>). <div eID="gen17707" type="x-p"/>
entries.b4cee060e48502ae8777447563c290890943b228: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9958"/><div sID="gen17708" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9958"/><hi type="bold">16. send for--</hi>translate, "I will send many"; "I will give the commission to many" (<reference osisRef="2Chr.17.7">2Ch 17:7</reference>).<div eID="gen17708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17709" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fishers ... hunters--</hi>successive invaders of Judea (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.2">Am 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.1.14">Ha 1:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.15">15</reference>). So "net" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.13">Eze 12:13</reference>). As to "hunters," see <reference osisRef="Gen.10.9">Ge 10:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.2">Mi 7:2</reference>. The Chaldees were famous in hunting, as the Egyptians, the other enemy of Judea, were in fishing. "Fishers" expresses the ease of their victory over the Jews as that of the angler over fishes; "hunters," the keenness of their pursuit of them into every cave and nook. It is remarkable, the same image is used in a good sense of the Jews' restoration, implying that just as their enemies were employed by God to take them in hand for destruction, so the same shall be employed for their restoration (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.9">Eze 47:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.10">10</reference>). So spiritually, those once enemies by nature (fishermen many of them literally) were employed by God to be heralds of salvation, "catching men" for life (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.19">Mt 4:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.5.10">Lu 5:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.41">Ac 2:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">4:4</reference>); compare here <reference osisRef="Jer.16.19">Jr 16:19</reference>, "the Gentiles shall come unto thee" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.16">2Co 12:16</reference>). <div eID="gen17709" type="x-p"/>
entries.dfd1f7de6dc7a35e8ba3d047a9f3592c55c6dc95: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9959"/><div sID="gen17710" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9959"/>17. (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.19">Jr 32:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.5.21">Pr 5:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.15.3">15:3</reference>).<div eID="gen17710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17711" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their iniquity--</hi>the cause of God's judgments on them. <div eID="gen17711" type="x-p"/>
entries.9a0646d96c185011c0e9b60079326762cf7bb30c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9960"/><div sID="gen17712" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9960"/><hi type="bold">18. first ... double--</hi>Horsley translates, "I will recompense ... once and again"; literally, "the first time repeated": alluding to the two captivities--the Babylonian and the Roman. Maurer, "I will recompense their former iniquities (those long ago committed by their fathers) and their (own) repeated sins" (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.11">Jr 16:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.12">12</reference>). English Version gives a good sense, "First (before 'I bring them again into their land'), I will doubly (that is, fully and amply, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.18">Jr 17:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.2">Is 40:2</reference>) recompense."<div eID="gen17712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17713" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">carcasses--</hi>not sweet-smelling sacrifices acceptable to God, but "carcasses" offered to idols, an offensive odor to God: human victims (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.5">Jr 19:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.20">Eze 16:20</reference>), and unclean animals (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.4">Is 65:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.17">66:17</reference>). Maurer explains it, "the carcasses" of the idols: their images void of sense and life. Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.16.19">Jr 16:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.20">20</reference>. <reference osisRef="Lev.26.30">Le 26:30</reference> favors this. <div eID="gen17713" type="x-p"/>
entries.184447dd21010e2eade6f8d44f69feb88710d5ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9961"/><div sID="gen17714" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9961"/>19-20. The result of God's judgments on the Jews will be that both the Jews when restored, and the Gentiles who have witnessed those judgments, shall renounce idolatry for the worship of Jehovah. Fulfilled partly at the return from Babylon, after which the Jews entirely renounced idols, and many proselytes were gathered in from the Gentiles, but not to be realized in its fulness till the final restoration of Israel (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.1-Isa.2.17">Is 2:1-17</reference>). <div eID="gen17714" type="x-p"/>
entries.63e6b11c8b5377b4e636ed57d5901a3c6db92a39: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9963"/><div sID="gen17717" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9963"/><hi type="bold">21. Therefore--</hi>In order that all may be turned from idols to Jehovah, He will now give awful proof of His divine power in the judgments He will inflict.<div eID="gen17717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17718" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">this once--</hi>If the punishments I have heretofore inflicted have not been severe enough to teach them.<div eID="gen17718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17719" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my name ... Lord--</hi>Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.18">Psa 83:18</reference>): God's incommunicable name, to apply which to idols would be blasphemy. Keeping His threats and promises (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.3">Ex 6:3</reference>). <chapter eID="Jer.16"/>

entries.74ebc8ccaebc3c532208f41b307859d01be29657: <div eID="gen29691" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen29692" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29693" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29693" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29692" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29694" type="x-p"/> On account of the evils which threatened his country, the prophet is forbidden to encumber himself with a wife and family, or to bear any share in the little joys and sorrows of his neighbors, which were to be forgotten and absorbed in those public calamities, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.1-Jer.16.9">Jer 16:1-9</reference>, which their sins should draw on them, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.10-Jer.16.13">Jer 16:10-13</reference>. A future restoration however is intimated, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.14">Jer 16:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.15">Jer 16:15</reference>, after these calamities should be endured, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.16-Jer.16.18">Jer 16:16-18</reference>; and the conversion of the Gentiles is foretold, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.19-Jer.16.21">Jer 16:19-21</reference>. <div eID="gen29694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29695" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen29695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29696" type="x-p"/> The word of the Lord came also unto me - This discourse Dahler supposes to have been delivered some time in the reign of Jehoiakim.
entries.06e5da9db7354e392832b6f19ea6b55a4d5a2686: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen29696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29697" type="x-p"/> Those shalt not take thee a wife - As it would be very inconvenient to have a family when the threatened desolations should come on the place. The reason is given in the following verses.
entries.5184c061eef6e5b4d516c139ff95668e8158cf25: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen29697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29698" type="x-p"/> They shall die of grievous deaths - All prematurely; see <reference osisRef="Jer.14.16">Jer 14:16</reference>. <div eID="gen29698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29699" type="x-p"/> As dung upon the face of the earth - See <reference osisRef="Jer.8.2">Jer 8:2</reference>. <div eID="gen29699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29700" type="x-p"/> Be meat for the fowls - See <reference osisRef="Jer.7.33">Jer 7:33</reference>.
entries.31d67c0cfd517f66fa45c4cf8cc5e44b4cd8b0ba: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen29700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29701" type="x-p"/> Enter not into the house of mourning - The public calamities are too great to permit individual losses to come into consideration.
entries.1effd195611b8da96076f3c44cf6a38eb166d2ae: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen29701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29702" type="x-p"/> Nor cut themselves - A custom of the heathen forbidden to the Jews, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.28">Lev 19:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deu.14.1">Deu 14:1</reference>, and which appears now to have prevailed among them; because, having become idolaters, they conformed to all the customs of the heathen. They tore their hair, rent their garments, cut their hands, arms, and faces. These were not only signs of sorrow but were even supposed to give ease to the dead, and appease the angry deities. The Hindoos, on the death of a relation, express their grief by loud lamentations, and not unfrequently bruise themselves in an agony of grief with whatever they can lay hold on.
entries.3715667bf0329b71d33b810e3ba370f19a4549ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen29702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29703" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt not also go into the house of feasting - Funeral banquets were made to commemorate the dead, and comfort the surviving relatives; and the cup of consolation, strong mingled wine, was given to those who were deepest in distress, to divert their minds and to soothe their sorrows. These kinds of ceremonies were common among almost all the nations of the world on funeral occasions. The Canaanites, the Jews, the Persians, Arabians, New Zealanders, Huns, etc., etc.
entries.2fb42d62548e5a84bfe2d87a1f49cb4d7d16409c: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen29703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29704" type="x-p"/> And ye have done worse than your fathers - The sins of the fathers would not have been visited on the children, had they not followed their example, and become even worse than they.
entries.167ef77156d4e5e8b55c3feeb1899bd3205b2066: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen29704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29705" type="x-p"/> Will I cast you out of this land - See <reference osisRef="Jer.7.15">Jer 7:15</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jer.9.15">Jer 9:15</reference>.
entries.f033b9866dfb7331e4637418ecaf5337807daf8a: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen29705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29706" type="x-p"/> The Lord liveth, that brought up - See <reference osisRef="Isa.43.18">Isa 43:18</reference>.
entries.30dd8ba431bc571a50bb4ca4726f70f1804be833: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen29706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29707" type="x-p"/> The land of the north - Chaldea: and their deliverance thence will be as remarkable as the deliverance of their fathers from the land of Egypt.
entries.00075d0710147259a6e3184a5669f28b7171e2c6: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen29707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29708" type="x-p"/> I will send for many fishers - for many hunters - I shall raise up enemies against them some of whom shall destroy them by wiles, and others shall ruin them by violence. This seems to be the meaning of these symbolical fishers and hunters.
entries.696397483bad996503c780f16454a4e175aeba8e: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen29708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29709" type="x-p"/> The carcasses of their detestable - things - Either meaning the idols themselves, which were only carcasses without life; or the sacrifices which were made to them.
entries.a12e06f2e1f3067eea56e85d1679dd7e2206627e: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen29709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29710" type="x-p"/> The Gentiles shall come - Even the days shall come when the Gentiles themselves, ashamed of their confidence, shall renounce their idols, and acknowledge that their fathers had believed lies, and worshipped vanities. This may be a prediction of the calling of the Gentiles by the Gospel of Christ; if so, it is a light amidst much darkness. In such dismal accounts there is need of some gracious promise relative to an amended state of the world.
entries.c651ba75f9d01c1ea505b11e4770f9b28fa31147: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen29710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29711" type="x-p"/> Shall a man make gods unto himself? - Can any be so silly, and so preposterously absurd? Yes, fallen man is capable of any thing that is base, mean, vile, and wicked, till influenced and converted by the grace of Christ.
entries.cdef45d40f5f1b7d0b483ab3832d236c9b276447: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen29711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29712" type="x-p"/> Therefore, behold, I will this once - I will not now change my purpose. They shall be visited and carried into captivity; nothing shall prevent this: and they shall know that my name is Jehovah. Since they would not receive the abundance of my mercies, they shall know what the true God can do in the way of judgment.  <chapter eID="Jer.16"/> <div eID="gen29712" type="x-p"/>

entries.ba09a7e15c3fb4e16538cae80d630661ae2e36e8: <reference osisRef="Jer.16.1-Jer.16.4">Jer 16:1-4</reference> <hi type="italic">The course to be pursued by the prophet with reference to the approaching judgment.</hi> - Jer 16:1. <hi type="italic">"And the word of Jahveh cam to me, saying: </hi> Jer 16:2. <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not take thee a wife, neither shalt thou have sons or daughters in this place. </hi> Jer 16:3. <hi type="italic">For thus hath Jahveh said concerning the sons and the daughters that are born in this place, and concerning their mothers that bear them, and concerning their fathers that beget them in this land: </hi> Jer 16:4. <hi type="italic">By deadly suffering shall they die, be neither lamented or buried; dung upon the field shall they become; and by sword and by famine shall they be consumed, and their carcases shall be meat for the fowls of the heavens and the beasts of the field. </hi> Jer 16:5. <hi type="italic">For thus hath Jahveh said: Come not into the house of mourning, and go not to lament, and bemoan them not; for I have taken away my peace from this people, saith Jahveh, grace and mercies. </hi> Jer 16:6. <hi type="italic">And great and small shall die in this land, not be buried; they shall not lament them, nor cut themselves, nor make themselves bald for them. </hi> Jer 16:7. <hi type="italic">And they shall not break bread for them in their mourning, to comfort one for the dead; nor shall they give to any the cup of comfort for his father and his mother. </hi> Jer 16:8. <hi type="italic">And into the house of feasting go not, to sit by them, to eat and to drink. </hi> Jer 16:9. <hi type="italic">For thus hath spoken Jahveh of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I cause to cease out of this place before your eyes, and in your days, the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride."</hi> <div eID="gen14020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14021" type="x-p"/> What the prophet is here bidden to do and to forbear is closely bound up with the proclamation enjoined on him of judgment to come on sinful Judah. This connection is brought prominently forward in the reasons given for these commands. He is neither to take a wife nor to beget children, because all the inhabitants of the land, sons and daughters, mothers and fathers, are to perish by sickness, the sword, and famine (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.3">Jer 16:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.16.4">Jer 16:4</reference>). He is both to abstain from the customary usages of mourning for the dead, and to keep away from mirthful feasts, in order to give the people to understand that, by reason of the multitude of the dead, customary mourning will have to be given up, and that all opportunity for merry-making will disappear (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.5-Jer.16.9">Jer 16:5-9</reference>). Adapting thus his actions to help to convey his message, he will approve himself to be the mouth of the Lord, and then the promised divine protection will not fail. Thus closely is this passage connected with the preceding complaint and reproof of the prophet (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.10-Jer.15.21">Jer 15:10-21</reference>), while it at the same time further continues the threatening of judgment in <reference osisRef="Jer.15.1">Jer 15:1</reference>-9. - With the prohibition to take a wife, cf. the apostle’s counsel, 1Co 7:26. "This place" alternates with "this land," and so must not be limited to Jerusalem, but bears on Judah at large. ילּדים, <hi type="italic">adject. verbale</hi>, as in Ex. 1:32. The form ממותי is found, besides here, only in <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.8">Eze 28:8</reference>, where it takes the place of מותי, Jer 16:10. תחלאים  ממותי, lit., deaths of sicknesses or sufferings, i.e., deaths by all kinds of sufferings, since תחלאים is not to be confined to disease, but in <reference osisRef="Jer.14.18">Jer 14:18</reference> is used of pining away by famine. With "they shall not be lamented," cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.25.33">Jer 25:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.8.2">Jer 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.16">Jer 14:16</reference>; Jer 7:33.
entries.a58cece151b19569f805a1c1084746e4e75346b4: <reference osisRef="Jer.16.5-Jer.16.6">Jer 16:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen14021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14022" type="x-p"/> The command not to go into a house of mourning (מרזח, loud crying, cry of lament for one dead, see on <reference osisRef="Amos.6.7">Amo 6:7</reference>), not to show sympathy with the survivors, is explained by the Lord in the fearfully solemn saying: I withdraw from this people my peace, grace, and mercy. שׁלום is not "the inviolateness of the relation between me and my people" (Graf), but the pace of God which rested on Judah, the source of its well-being, of its life and prosperity, and which showed itself to the sinful race in the extension to them of grace and mercy. The consequence of the withdrawal of this peace is the death of great and small in such multitudes that they can neither be buried nor mourned for (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.6">Jer 16:6</reference>). התגּדד, but one’s self, is used in <reference osisRef="Deut.14.1">Deu 14:1</reference> for נתן שׂרט, to make cuts in the body, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.28">Lev 19:28</reference>; and קרח, <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>., to crop one’s self bald, acc. to <reference osisRef="Deut.14.1">Deu 14:1</reference>, to shave a bare place on the front part of the head above the eyes. These are two modes of expressing passionate mourning for the dead which were forbidden to the Israelites in the law, yet which remained in use among the people, see on <reference osisRef="Lev.19.28">Lev 19:28</reference> and Deu 14:1. להם, for them, in honour of the dead.
entries.a1825e1804b94de0f264bdc47c1b24f5bf9c11e2: <reference osisRef="Jer.16.7">Jer 16:7</reference> פּרס, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.58.7">Isa 58:7</reference>, for פּרשׂ, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.4">Lam 4:4</reference>, break, sc. the bread (cf. Isa. <hi type="italic">l.c</hi>.) for mourning, and to give to drink the cup of comfort, does not refer to the meals which were held in the house of mourning upon occasion of a death after the interment, for this custom cannot be proved of the Israelites in Old Testament times, and is not strictly demanded by the words of the verse. To break bread to any one does not mean to hold a feast with him, but to bestow a gift of bread upon him; cf. Isa 58:7. Correspondingly, to give to drink, does not here mean to drink to one’s health at a feast, but only to present with wine to drink. The words refer to the custom of sending bread and wine for refreshment into the house of the surviving relatives of one dead, to comfort them in their sorrow; cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.35">2Sa 3:35</reference>; 2Sa 12:16., and the remarks on Eze 24:17. The singular suffixes on לנחמו, אביו, and אמּו, alongside of the plurals להם and אותם, are to be taken distributively of every one who is to be comforted upon occasion of a death in his house; and להם is not to be changed, as by J. D. Mich. and Hitz., into לחם.
entries.ec31092d3f7ecc49ee9a29177a73a17e934daf87: <reference osisRef="Jer.16.8-Jer.16.9">Jer 16:8-9</reference> <div eID="gen14022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14023" type="x-p"/> The prophet is to withdraw from all participation in mirthful meals and feasts, in token that God will take away all joy from the people. בּית־משׁתּה, house in which a feast is given. אותם, for אתּם, refers, taken <hi type="italic">ad sensum</hi>, to the others who take part in the feast. On <reference osisRef="Jer.16.9">Jer 16:9</reference>, cf. Jer 7:34.
entries.455163a485f3b5ab1e6502f7e0dd0bffe7447fbd: <reference osisRef="Jer.16.10-Jer.16.15">Jer 16:10-15</reference> <hi type="italic">"And when thou showest this people all these things, and they say unto thee, Wherefore hath Jahveh pronounced all this great evil against us, and what is our transgression, and what our sin that we have committed against Jahveh our God?</hi> Jer 16:11. <hi type="italic">Then say thou to them, Because your fathers have forsaken me, saith Jahveh, and have walked after other gods, and served them, and worshipped them, and have forsaken me, and not kept my law;</hi> Jer 16:12. <hi type="italic">And ye did yet worse than your fathers; and behold, ye walk each after the stubbornness of his evil heart, hearkening not unto me.</hi> Jer 16:13. <hi type="italic">Therefore I cast you out of this land into the land which he know not, neither ye nor your fathers, and there may ye serve other gods day and night, because I will show you no favour.</hi> Jer 16:14. <hi type="italic">Therefore, behold, the days come, saith Jahveh, that it shall no more be said, By the life of Jahveh, that brought up the sons of Israel out of the land of Egypt,</hi> Jer 16:15. <hi type="italic">But, By the life of Jahveh, that brought the sons of Israel out of the land of the north, and out of all the lands whither I had driven them, and I bring them again into their land that I gave to their fathers."</hi> <div eID="gen14023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14024" type="x-p"/> The turn of the discourse in <reference osisRef="Jer.16.10">Jer 16:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.16.11">Jer 16:11</reference> is like that in Jer 5:19. With <reference osisRef="Jer.16.11">Jer 16:11</reference> cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.11.8">Jer 11:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.10">Jer 11:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.24">Jer 7:24</reference>; with "ye did yet worse," etc., cf. 1Ki 14:9; and on "after the stubbornness," cf. on 1Ki 3:17. The apodosis begins with "therefore I cast you out." On this head cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.7.15">Jer 7:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.9.15">Jer 9:15</reference>, and Jer 22:26. The article in על־הארץ, Graf quite unnecessarily insists on having cancelled, as out of place. It is explained sufficiently by the fact, that the land, of which mention has so often been made, is looked on as a specific one, and is characterized by the following relative clause, as one unknown to the people. Besides, the "ye know not" is not meant of geographical ignorance, but, as is often the case with ידע, the knowledge is that obtained by direct experience. They know not the land, because they have never been there. "There ye may serve them," Ros. justly characterizes as <hi type="italic">concessio cum ironia</hi>: there ye may serve, as long as ye will, the gods whom ye have so longed after. The irony is especially marked in the "day and night." Here Jeremiah has in mind <reference osisRef="Deut.4.28">Deu 4:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.36">Deu 28:36</reference>, Deu 28:63. אשׁר is causal, giving the grounds of the threat, "I cast you out." The form חנינה is hap leg . - In <reference osisRef="Jer.16.14">Jer 16:14</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.16.15">Jer 16:15</reference> the prophet opens to the people a view of ultimate redemption from the affliction amidst the heathen, into which, for their sin, they will be cast. By and by men will swear no more by Jahveh who redeemed them out of Egypt, but by Jahveh who has brought them again from the land of the north and the other lands into which they have been thrust forth. In this is implied that this second deliverance will be a blessing which shall outshine the former blessing of redemption from Egypt. But just as this deliverance will excel the earlier one, so much the greater will the affliction of Israel in the northern land be than the Egyptian bondage had been. On this point Ros. throws especial weight, remarking that the aim of these verses is not so much to give promise of coming salvation, as to announce <hi type="italic">instare illis atrocius malum, quam illud Aegyptiacum, eamque quam mox sint subituri servitutem multo fore duriorem, quam olim Aegyptiaca fuerit</hi>. But though this idea does lie <hi type="italic">implicite</hi> in the words, yet we must not fail to be sure that the prospect held out of a future deliverance of Israel from the lands into which it is soon to be scattered, and of its restoration again to the land of its fathers, has, in the first and foremost place, a comforting import, and that it is intended to preserve the godly from despair under the catastrophe which is now awaiting them.<note placement="foot">Calvin has excellently brought out both moments, and has thus expounded the thought of the passage: <hi type="italic">"Scitis unde patres vestri exierint, nempe e fornace aenea, quemadmodum alibi loquitur (xi. 4) et quasi ex profunda morte; itaque redemptio illa debuit esse memorabilis usque ad finem mundi. Sed jam Deus conjiciet vos in abyssum, quae longe profundior erit illa Aegypti tyrannide, e qua erepti sunt patres vestri; nam si inde vos redimat, erit miraculum longe excellentius ad posteros, ut fere exstinguat vel saltem obscuret memoriam prioris illius redemptionis."</hi></note> לכן is not <hi type="italic">nevertheless</hi>, but, as universally, <hi type="italic">therefore</hi>; and the train of thought is as follows: Because the Lord will, for their idolatry, cast forth His people into the lands of the heathen, just for that very reason will their redemption from exile not fail to follow, and this deliverance surpass in gloriousness the greatest of all former deeds of blessing, the rescue of Israel from Egypt. The prospect of future redemption given amidst announcements of judgment cannot be surprising in Jeremiah, who elsewhere also interweaves the like happy forecastings with his most solemn threatenings; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.4.27">Jer 4:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.10">Jer 5:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.5.18">Jer 5:18</reference>, with Jer 3:14., Jer 23:3., etc. "This ray of light, falling suddenly into the darkness, does not take us more by surprise than 'I will not make a full end,' Jer 4:27. There is therefore no reason for regarding these two verses as interpolations from <reference osisRef="Jer.23.7">Jer 23:7</reference>-8" (Graf).<hi type="italic">Further account of the punishment foretold, with the reasons for the same. -</hi> Jer 16:16. <hi type="italic">"Behold, I send for many fishers, saith Jahve, who shall fish them, and after will I send fore many hunters, who shall hunt them from every mountain and every hill, and out of the clefts of the rock.</hi> Jer 16:17. <hi type="italic">For mine eyes are upon all their ways, they are not hidden from me, neither is their iniquity concealed from mine eyes.</hi> Jer 16:18. <hi type="italic">And first, I requite double their iniquity and their sin, because they defiled my land with the carcases of their detestables, and with their abominations they have filled mine inheritance.</hi> Jer 16:19. <hi type="italic">Jahveh, my strength and my fortress, and my refuge in the day of trouble! Unto Thee shall the peoples come from the ends of the earth and say: But lies have our fathers inherited, vanity, and amidst them none profiteth at all.</hi> Jer 16:20. <hi type="italic">Shall a man make gods to himself, which are yet no gods?</hi> Jer 16:21. <hi type="italic">Therefore, behold, I make them to know this once, I make them to know my hand and my might, and they shall know that my name is Jahveh."</hi>
entries.32f6b0d362a6ff4d396d622f1b663193fd1d03ed: <reference osisRef="Jer.16.16-Jer.16.17">Jer 16:16-17</reference> <div eID="gen14024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14025" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Jer.16.16-Jer.16.18">Jer 16:16-18</reference> are a continuation of the threatening in <reference osisRef="Jer.16.13">Jer 16:13</reference>, that Judah is to be cast out, but are directly connected with <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Jer.16.15">Jer 16:15</reference></hi>, and elucidate the expulsion into many lands there foretold. The figures of the fishers and hunters do not bespeak the gathering again and restoration of the scattered people, as Ven. would make out, but the carrying of Judah captive out of his land. This is clear from the second of the figures, for the hunter does not gather the animals together, but kills them; and the reference of the verses is put beyond a doubt by <reference osisRef="Jer.16.17">Jer 16:17</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.16.18">Jer 16:18</reference>, and is consequently admitted by all other comm. The two figures signify various kinds of treatment at the hands of enemies. The fishers represent the enemies that gather the inhabitants of the land as in a net, and carry them wholesale into captivity (cf. <reference osisRef="Amos.4.2">Amo 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.1.15">Hab 1:15</reference>). The hunters, again, are those who drive out from their hiding-places, and slay or carry captive such as have escaped from the cities, and have taken refuge in the mountains and ravines; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.4.29">Jer 4:29</reference>, Jdg 6:2 1Sa 13:6. In this the idea is visibly set forth that none shall escape the enemy. שׁלה <hi type="italic">c</hi>. ל <hi type="italic">pers</hi>., send for one, cause him to come, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.14.3">Jer 14:3</reference> (send for water), so that there is no call to take ל according to the Aram. usage as sign of the accusative, for which we can cite in Jeremiah only the case in Jer 40:2. The form דּוּגים (<hi type="italic">Chet</hi>.) agrees with <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.10">Eze 47:10</reference>, while the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi>, דּיּגים, is a formation similar to ציּדים. In the second clause רבּים is, like the numerals, made to precede the noun; cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.31.29">Pro 31:29</reference>; Psa 89:51. - For the Lord knows their doings and dealings, and their transgressions are not hid from Him; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.23.24">Jer 23:24</reference>; Jer 32:19. על for אל, indicating the direction. Their ways are not the ways of flight, but their course of action.
entries.fe6caf0254e435e33500a3a89c1d0fd08b9a7ec5: <reference osisRef="Jer.16.18">Jer 16:18</reference>  The punishment foretold is but retribution for their sins. Because they have defiled the land by idolatry, they shall be driven out of it. ראשׁונה, first, is by Jerome, Hitz., Ew., Umbr. made to refer to the salvation promised in <reference osisRef="Jer.16.15">Jer 16:15</reference> : first, i.e., before the restoration of my favour spoken of in <reference osisRef="Jer.16.15">Jer 16:15</reference>, I requite double. Against this Graf has objected, that on this view "first" would appear somewhat superfluous; and Näg., that the manifestly intended antithesis to משׁנה is left out of account. There is little force in either objection. Even Näg.'s paraphrase does not do full justice to the presumed antithesis; for if we render: "For the first time the double shall be requited, in the event of repetition a severer standard shall be used," then the antithesis to "first" would not be "double," but the supplied repetition of the offence. There is not the slightest hint in the context to lead us to supply this idea; nor is there any antithesis between "first" and "double." It is a mere assumption of the comm., which Rashi, Kimchi, Ros., Maur., etc., have brought into the text by the interpolation of a ו <hi type="italic">cop</hi>. before משׁנה: I requite the first of their transgressions and the repetition of them, i.e., their earlier and their repeated sins, or the sins committed by their fathers and by themselves, on a greater scale.
